This release improves jewelry, metal and gem rendering, makes scene updates and camera settings cheaper, and stores the new rendering options in settings version 7.2.

#### Rendering

- Added the bloom property `highlightsOnly` (SS-10493). When enabled, only the light above `luminanceThreshold` blooms (soft knee of width `luminanceSmoothing`, per-pixel cap, tighter mipmap blur), so only highlights glow and bright metal keeps its colour. Unset `luminanceThreshold`, `luminanceSmoothing` and `mipmapBlur` then default to 1, 0.25 and true. With 8-bit buffers the threshold is capped at 0.8. Recommended together with `hdr` and Neutral tone mapping. Existing models and bloom without the property render unchanged.
- Added the bloom property `highlightLimit` (SS-10533, default 8). With `highlightsOnly` and `hdr`, it is the most bloom light a single pixel can add, in multiples of white. Very bright gems can leave a pale glow on the metal around them; a lower value (e.g. 1) removes it and keeps a small glow on the gems. Settings version 7.2 stores it; bloom without the property renders unchanged.
- Added the bloom property `additiveBlur` (SS-10603, default false), stored in settings 7.2. With mipmap blur, the blur levels are added instead of blended: the glow reaches over three octaves and, at the same `intensity`, adds about 2.4 times the light above `luminanceThreshold`, like the additive bloom of other renderers. Small, very bright highlights such as gem glints then get a visible glow. The blur radius has no effect with it, and `highlightLimit` caps the light before the blur. Meant for `hdr`: with 8-bit buffers each blur level is clipped at white. Bloom without the property renders unchanged. The `jewelry` preset uses it: gem glints in close-ups get the glow of the WebGi reference with the same environment map (before: 2 to 6 levels less), and overview shots of polished gold get 3 to 5 levels brighter. The default settings and the other presets do not use it; to get the previous look of the `jewelry` preset, remove `additiveBlur` from its bloom.
- Settings version 7.2 stores the new rendering options (SS-10497): `postprocessing.hdr`, the bloom properties `backgroundBloom` and `highlightsOnly`, `environment.mapPbrMode`, `environment.mapOrientation`, `environment.mapAnalyticDfg`, `material.physicalGemDispersion`, `material.gemTracing`, `material.gemNormalMapResolution`, and the HBAO/SSAO properties `mode` and `excludeGems`. Settings saved before 7.2 are converted with the old-look values, so existing models render unchanged.
- Added the HBAO and SSAO property `excludeGems` (SS-10497, default false). With `false`, gems are darkened by the composite ambient occlusion as before the gem exclusion of 3.23; set it to `true` to keep gems out of the ambient occlusion. The "shading" mode never darkens gems.
- Added the viewport property `physicalGemDispersion` (SS-10495, default false). When enabled, gem `refractionIndex` is the mid-spectrum (D line) value and `dispersion` is n(G line) − n(B line) (diamond 0.044); each colour channel uses its own refraction index when light enters, inside the stone and when it leaves, so blue bends most. Existing models keep the legacy dispersion, where `dispersion` offsets 1 / IOR by `dispersion * 0.025` per channel at entry only.
- Added the viewport properties `gemTracing` ("sphere" default, "facets") and `gemNormalMapResolution` (default 1024) (SS-10495). Facet-plane gem tracing and 512 px gem normal maps from 3.23 (SS-10470) are now opt-in; without them gems render as in 3.22. A gem material's `normalMapResolution` no longer defaults to 512; when unset the viewport value applies.
- Added the viewport properties `physicalGemFresnel` (default false) and `gemEnvironmentMapIntensity` (default 1) (SS-10532), stored in settings 7.2 as `material.physicalGemFresnel` and `material.gemEnvironmentMapIntensity`. With `physicalGemFresnel`, most light inside a gem leaves at the first facet it can pass (1 − Fresnel reflectance) instead of bouncing on, which gives larger, calmer facets like a real brilliant. `gemEnvironmentMapIntensity` scales the environment light of gems only, to match the stones to the scene for a given environment map. Existing models keep the legacy weights and the factor 1; the default settings use `physicalGemFresnel = true` and `gemEnvironmentMapIntensity = 1.2`.
- Added the viewport property `gemLighting` (SS-10505, SS-10602; "all" default, "firstSurface", "environment"), stored in settings 7.2 as `material.gemLighting`. With "firstSurface", gems evaluate the point, spot, directional and rect-area lights on the first surface only; light that bounces inside the stone uses the environment and ambient light, which makes the gem shader smaller and faster to compile. With "environment", gems ignore every scene light, including ambient and hemisphere lights, on the first surface and inside the stone: the environment map is their only light, which gives darker facets and more contrast. Existing models keep "all"; the default settings and presets use "environment".
- Added the viewport property `gemClampColor` (SS-10604, default true), stored in settings 7.2 as `material.gemClampColor`. Without the HDR composer (no post-processing effect, or `hdr` off) gems clamp each traced color at 1, so after tone mapping no stone pixel reaches white. With `gemClampColor = false` the colors are not clamped and the highlights of the stones reach white also in viewports without effects. With `hdr` and at least one effect nothing changes. Existing models keep the clamp; the default settings and presets turn it off.
- Added the gem material properties `attenuationColor` (default white) and `attenuationDistance` (default `Infinity`, in model units) (SS-10496). They have the same names and meaning as in three.js `MeshPhysicalMaterial` and the glTF volume extension: light inside the stone takes on `attenuationColor` after it has traveled `attenuationDistance`, per color channel. Thick parts of a coloured stone get more saturated than thin ones. The path is measured in world units, so scaled and mirrored stones absorb like unscaled ones. It works on top of `colorTransferBegin` / `colorTransferEnd`. With the default distance the absorption is off and its shader code is left out, so existing gems render as before; no preset sets it.
- Added the viewport property `environmentMapOrientation` (SS-10522, "legacy" default, "threejs"). With "threejs", custom `.hdr` environment maps have the same orientation as in three.js and other tools; built-in presets render the same in both modes. Existing models keep the legacy orientation.
- New look for viewers without stored settings and for the settings presets (SS-10494). The default settings (`defaultSettings`, used by new models, by models without stored settings and by viewports created without settings) are now settings 7.2 with these values. Each one can be turned off with the option named in brackets:
    - `hdr` on (`postprocessing.hdr = false`), only in the `default`, `jewelry` and `furniture` presets; devices without half-float render targets keep 8-bit buffers. The presets without tone mapping (`medical`, `highPerformance`, `twoDimensional`) keep it off.
    - ambient occlusion leaves gems out (HBAO/SSAO `excludeGems = false`).
    - modern PBR environment shading (`environmentMapPbrMode = "legacy"`).
    - three.js orientation for custom `.hdr` maps (`environmentMapOrientation = "legacy"`).
    - physical gem dispersion (`physicalGemDispersion = false`), facet-plane gem tracing (`gemTracing = "sphere"`) and 512 px gem normal maps (`gemNormalMapResolution = 1024`).
    - physical Fresnel weights inside gems (`physicalGemFresnel = false`) and gem reflections at 1.2 (`gemEnvironmentMapIntensity = 1`).
    - gems lit by the environment map only, without the scene lights (`gemLighting = "all"`).
    - gem highlights that reach white without post-processing effects (`gemClampColor = true`).
- The `jewelry` preset additionally uses HBAO, a weak bloom on highlights only without background bloom (`highlightsOnly`, `backgroundBloom`, intensity 0.2, `luminanceThreshold` 2, `luminanceSmoothing` 0.5), ACES Filmic tone mapping with exposure 1, and SMAA on mobile instead of FXAA (SS-10494).
- With `hdr` on and half-float buffers, a bloom without `blendFunction` is now added to the image (`ADD`) instead of screened (`SCREEN`). In a half-float buffer the screen blend took light away from pixels brighter than white, which made polished metal darker. With 8-bit buffers (`hdr` off, every model with settings stored before 7.2) nothing changes. Set `blendFunction` to `SCREEN` to get the old blend back.
- Added the viewport property `environmentMapAnalyticDfg` (default false), stored in settings 7.2 as `environment.mapAnalyticDfg`. It uses the analytic formula of older three.js versions for how much of the environment a surface reflects, instead of the lookup table of current three.js; polished metal gets slightly brighter (about 1.5 levels on gold). It only changes the environment reflection, independent of `environmentMapPbrMode`; in the "legacy" PBR mode it changes nothing. Existing models and the default settings keep it off.
- The `jewelry` preset now uses the HBAO "shading" mode (ambient occlusion only on the indirect light, so the mirror reflections of polished metal are no longer darkened) and `environmentMapAnalyticDfg`. Together with the bloom blend above, polished gold in close-ups is now about as bright as in the WebGi reference with the same environment map (before: 5 to 9 levels darker). Its bloom and tone mapping are the ones of that reference; they may be tuned again when further jewelry features are added. To get the previous look of the preset, remove `mode` from the HBAO effect, set `environmentMapAnalyticDfg = false` and give the bloom `blendFunction: SCREEN`.
- Settings version 7.2 stores the largest drawing buffer as `rendering.maximumRenderingSize` (desktop) and `rendering.maximumRenderingSizeMobile` (SS-10506); the viewport property `maximumRenderingSize` is the value of the current device. The default settings (`default`, `jewelry`, `furniture`, `medical`, `twoDimensional`) raise the desktop value from 1920×1080 to 2560×1440, so large viewports on HiDPI screens are sharper; `highPerformance` and mobile keep their sizes. Set `maximumRenderingSize` to change it.
- Added the post-processing effect `ssr`, screen-space reflections (SS-10509). Polished metal (opaque, metalness above 0.5, roughness up to `maxRoughness`) reflects the neighbouring geometry it can see on screen, for example the gallery under a ring's head or the inner faces of prongs, instead of only the environment map; where the reflected ray hits nothing on screen, the environment reflection stays. The reflections are computed inside the material shading from the previous frame, so they need HDR (`hdr`) for highlights above white; a frame without a previous one (new effect, resize, screenshot) is drawn twice. Gems, transparent and specular-glossiness materials do not receive them. Properties: `intensity` (1), `maxRoughness` (0.3), `steps` (16), `distance` (2) and `thickness` (0.2) relative to the scene size like the HBAO `distance`, and `enableOnMobile` (false). Settings version 7.2 stores the effect. The `jewelry` preset uses it on desktop (not on mobile devices); the engine default, the other presets and settings stored before 7.2 do not, so those models render unchanged. On the jewelry example ring it brings the gold within about 2.6 levels of the reference renderer's reflections and costs 3 to 12 % frame time on a desktop GPU. To get the previous look of the `jewelry` preset, remove the `ssr` effect.
- Added the HBAO and SSAO property `specularOcclusion` (SS-10601; "physical" default, "uniform"), stored in settings 7.2. It only applies in the "shading" mode. With "physical", the ambient occlusion reaches the environment reflections through the specular occlusion of three.js, which leaves polished metal seen head-on almost untouched and darkens it to nearly black at grazing angles. With "uniform", the reflections are darkened by the ambient occlusion itself, like the ambient light. The `jewelry` preset now uses SSAO with `mode: "shading"` and `specularOcclusion: "uniform"` instead of HBAO: on a ring it darkens the gold within 2 levels of the WebGi reference on six camera shots (HBAO: up to 9 levels off) and no longer puts a dark band on the lower shank in the top view. To get the previous AO of the preset, replace the SSAO effect by `{type: "hbao", properties: {mode: "shading", excludeGems: true}}`. The other presets, the default settings and existing models render unchanged.
- Added the viewport property `accumulationMode` (SS-10607; "display" default, "hdr"), stored in settings 7.2 as `rendering.accumulationMode`. It sets where the frames of `accumulationFrames` are averaged. With "display", the finished frames are averaged on the canvas, after bloom and tone mapping, as before. With "hdr", the scene is averaged in the HDR buffer of the post-processing, before the effects and the tone mapping, which then run once on the average: a small highlight that covers a pixel in only some of the jittered frames keeps its full brightness instead of being clipped at white in every frame before it is averaged, so the brightest highlights on polished metal are crisper. "hdr" needs post-processing with `hdr` on a device with half-float render targets; otherwise "display" is used. The `jewelry` preset uses "hdr" (on the ring example with the same environment map as the WebGi reference, the frame accumulation now brightens the gold as much as the reference does, and the brightest tenth of the gold in the full jewelry pipeline gets 1 to 6 levels brighter, closer to the reference on all six test views). The default settings and the other presets keep "display"; existing models render unchanged. To get the previous look of the `jewelry` preset, set `accumulationMode = "display"`.
- Added the viewport property `environmentMapFiltering` (SS-10626; "ggx" default, "gaussian"), stored in settings 7.2 as `environment.mapFiltering`. It sets how the blurred levels of HDR environment maps are prefiltered. "ggx" is the GGX importance sampling of current three.js, as before. "gaussian" is the Gaussian blur of three.js r160 and older. The sharp level is the same in both, but polished metal also reads the blurred levels on thin, curved parts, so with "gaussian" polished gold gets about as bright as in renderers on older three.js. Changing it reloads the current environment map; cube maps of six images are not affected. The `jewelry` preset uses "gaussian": with no effect and the same environment map, the bare gold of the ring example is now within 0.8 levels of the WebGi reference on the mean (before: 0.5 to 2.5 levels darker). The default settings and the other presets keep "ggx"; existing models render unchanged. To get the previous look of the `jewelry` preset, set `environmentMapFiltering = "ggx"`.
- Added the viewport property `environmentMapSquaredRoughnessBend` (SS-10627; default false), stored in settings 7.2 as `environment.mapSquaredRoughnessBend`. For a rough reflection, three.js bends the reflection vector towards the surface normal; with this option it bends by roughness² like three.js r162 and older, instead of roughness⁴. Polished metal is affected on thin, curved parts, where three.js adds roughness against aliasing: the highlights land a fraction of a pixel elsewhere, the mean brightness stays. It only changes the bend, independent of `environmentMapPbrMode`; in the "legacy" PBR mode, which already bends by roughness², it changes nothing. The `jewelry` preset turns it on: together with the Gaussian environment filtering, the bare gold of the ring example differs per pixel from the WebGi reference by 0.3 to 0.8 levels on average instead of 1.7 to 2.9. The default settings and the other presets keep it off; existing models render unchanged. To get the previous look of the `jewelry` preset, set `environmentMapSquaredRoughnessBend = false`.
- Fixed: when the environment map was changed while another one was still loading, the map that finished loading last was shown, which could be the older one. The map set last is now shown (SS-10626).
- Fixed: with `environmentMapOrientation = "threejs"`, the diffuse light of custom `.hdr` environment maps (the irradiance) came from the side of the map mirrored in x, while the reflections came from the right side (SS-10634). The irradiance is now looked up in the same direction as the reflections. Built-in environment maps, cube maps of six images and the "legacy" orientation (the engine default and every model with settings stored before 7.2) render unchanged. Because "threejs" is the orientation of the 7.2 default settings, this changes every viewer with the 7.2 default settings or a preset and a custom `.hdr` map: rough and diffuse surfaces get their light from the correct side of the map, and polished gold on the ring example now matches the WebGi reference with no effect and the same environment map (mean difference 0.0 levels on six views, before up to 0.7). To get the previous look, set `environmentMapOrientation = "legacy"` (this also turns the map back by a quarter turn).
- Identical gem stones share one gem normal map, and maps nobody uses any more are freed (SS-10500). Stones with the same shape and normal map resolution are recognised even when they are separate meshes at different positions; the map no longer keeps a depth buffer after the capture, and removing one stone no longer breaks the map of the others. A pavé of 120 identical stones as separate meshes needs 3 maps (72 MB) instead of 122 maps (about 2.9 GB of colour plus as much depth) at 1024 px; the ring example keeps its 2 maps and drops 12 MB of depth buffers. A map that loses its last stone through a hover or selection material is freed after the next node removal. Stones look as before.
- Fixed: one gem material shared by stones of different shapes or positions rendered every stone with the normal map, center and radius of the first one, both on first load and when the material was assigned later (SS-10501). Each stone shape now gets its own gem material; stones of one shape still share one.
- Models with settings stored before 7.2 render unchanged. The engine defaults of all new options stay the old look.

#### Camera

- **Breaking:** setting a camera property only requests a frame (SS-10551, SS-10554). This covers `position`, `target`, `fov` (perspective), `direction` (orthographic) and all other `ICameraApi` properties (for example `zoomRestriction`, `enableTurntableControls`, `defaultPosition`, `damping`). The setters no longer run a scene update and no longer fire `VIEWPORT_UPDATED`; camera events still fire. Scene tree changes that were not applied with `update()` are applied by the next frame, not by the setter. The view also changes while `suspendSceneUpdates` is set.
    - Affected: code that listens to `VIEWPORT_UPDATED` to react to a camera setting, or that relies on a camera setter to apply scene tree changes made without `update()`.
    - Before: `camera.fov = 30; // VIEWPORT_UPDATED fired, scene tree changes were applied`
    - After: `camera.fov = 30; viewport.update(); // only if you need scene tree changes applied or the event`. To react to a camera that moves, listen to `CAMERA_MOVE` / `CAMERA_END` instead (only setters that move the camera fire them).
    - Checked: no example in ViewerExamples or AppBuilderSdk depends on it.
- **Breaking:** the camera moves by exactly what the input asks for, and the same on every display (SS-10628). Before, every pointer and wheel event moved the camera at once and the following frames repeated a fading copy of that step. A drag moved about 1.9 times the set speed, the camera drifted for 1 to 2 s after the pointer stopped with the button still down, and it coasted about 9 times the last step after the release. The repeat ran once per frame, so a wheel notch zoomed about twice as far and auto-rotation turned twice as fast on a 120 Hz display as on a 60 Hz one. Now the input moves a goal by the documented amount and the camera follows the goal with a time-based spring.
    - While a button or finger is down the camera stops about `movementSmoothness` × 100 ms after the pointer stops. After the release it continues with the speed of the pointer and slows down; releasing a pointer that stands still gives no inertia. Pressing a button or putting a finger down stops a camera that is still moving.
    - Auto-rotation, the length of the inertia and the distance of a wheel notch are the same at 30, 60, 120 and 144 Hz. A frame longer than 100 ms (hidden tab, stall) counts as 100 ms for the camera, and the first frame after the page was loaded as 0 ms.
    - Saved settings keep their values; what the values mean changes:

        | Setting              | Before                                                                                                                                                                              | Now                                                                                                                                           |
        | -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
        | `rotationSpeed`      | 0.5 = about half a turn per canvas height dragged at 60 Hz (touch 1.5 times that), depending on the event and frame rate                                                            | 0.5 = one full turn per canvas height dragged, for mouse and touch                                                                            |
        | `panSpeed`           | 0.5 = about 1.7 times the pointer distance (perspective, mouse), depending on the event and frame rate                                                                              | 0.5 = the point under the pointer at the depth of the target follows the pointer exactly (perspective, mouse and touch)                       |
        | `damping`            | fraction by which a repeated copy of each input step faded per 1/60 s; it also changed how far a drag, a wheel notch or a key press moved the camera (distance about 1 / `damping`) | inertia only: the remaining motion shrinks by this fraction every 1/60 s (0.1 = about 160 ms, 1 = none); the distances no longer depend on it |
        | `movementSmoothness` | blend factor between consecutive pointer events; no effect on the wheel                                                                                                             | time the camera needs to catch up with the pointer while a button or finger is down, as a fraction of 100 ms (0.5 = about 50 ms, 0 = exact)   |
        | `autoRotationSpeed`  | 1 = one full turn per minute at 60 Hz, twice as fast at 120 Hz                                                                                                                      | 1 = one full turn per minute on every display                                                                                                 |
        | `zoomSpeed` (wheel)  | 0.5 = about 12 % of the distance per notch at 60 Hz and `damping` 0.1, about twice as far at 120 Hz                                                                                 | 0.5 = about 12 % of the distance per notch on every display                                                                                   |
        | `keyPanSpeed`        | distance per key press depended on `damping` and the frame rate                                                                                                                     | one key press pans by `keyPanSpeed` / 2 pixels at `panSpeed` 0.5 (the former distance at 60 Hz and `damping` 0.1, times 1.14)                 |

    - Affected: every viewer feels different with unchanged settings. Rotation by mouse is about twice as fast as before at 60 Hz, panning a perspective camera by mouse about 0.6 times as fast (it now follows the pointer), and the camera no longer drifts. Viewers with a `damping` other than 0.1 keep today's inertia length but lose the side effect on the distances.
    - To keep the former rotation speed, halve `rotationSpeed`: `camera.rotationSpeed = 0.25; // was 0.5`. To pan faster than the pointer as before, set `camera.panSpeed = 0.8; // was 0.5`. To get a camera that stops at once, set `camera.damping = 1` and `camera.movementSmoothness = 0`.
    - Zoom by dragging (middle mouse button, pinch) and panning an orthographic camera keep their factors but lose the repeated motion as well, so they are about half as fast as before; they are reworked in SS-10629.
    - Checked: AppBuilderSdk does not use these settings. ViewerExamples uses `autoRotationSpeed` in one example (`examples/materials/gem_material`, a slider from -10 to 10), which keeps working and now turns equally fast on every display.

#### Performance

- A scene update of one node costs work in proportion to that change, not to the size of the scene (SS-10550). Picking (`IntersectionEngine`), the interaction managers, the animation list and the camera search no longer read the whole scene tree on every `VIEWPORT_UPDATED`. Hiding or showing one object on a model with about 4,000 objects no longer reads the data of about 62,000 tree nodes (the counter `oneNodeChange.treeDataReads` goes from 61,997 to 45).
- `VIEWPORT_UPDATED` has a new optional field `sceneChanges` (SS-10550, `IViewportUpdatedEvent`, `ISceneChanges`): the nodes of the scene tree that the update of the viewport went through (`nodes`, parents before children) and the ids of the nodes that were removed from the viewport (`removedNodeIds`). The field is absent when the update went through the whole tree (first update of a viewport, change of the renderer type or of GPU instancing, attribute visualization) or when no scene update ran for the event. Listeners that keep their own data about the tree should read the whole tree then.
- Changes of a node that are made without `updateVersion()` (for example `visible`, `intersectionTest`, the `groupId` of interaction data or the name of animation data) are no longer picked up by picking, interaction and animations when another node is updated with `updateVersion()` in the same update; they are applied the next time that node is updated, or by an `update()` without any versioned change, which still reads the whole tree (SS-10550). Call `updateVersion()` after changing a node.
